doc.title: Ingrid Sertso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, August 11, 2014

title: Humor in free jazz
summary: Humor and lightheartedness are part of her music's openness.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong
story.community_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor

blocks.x: I think there’s part of our culture that we sometimes feel these kinds of artists ought to suffer and we take some kind of fascination in their life stories that are so difficult. You know, like it seems romantic almost. Charlie Parker burns out at age 36 or whatever. And it’s a shame. Yeah. Along those same lines, we talked about the seriousness of Billie Holiday. Is there a place in free jazz, the music you do, for humor and lightheartedness?
I don’t know what you mean. Of course.
Well okay. Some of the videos I watched, and some of the music — I had a very sort of jilting experience when I was just getting into John Coltrane, right? And someone said,
“Well you should get ‘Ascension,’ you should buy the record ‘Ascension.’” And then I got to free jazz. Well this music, I couldn’t handle it. It sounded chaotic to me.
But when you do the thing with the large ensemble and the music is taking shape, it seems serious to me, which isn’t a bad thing, but does it ever get to the point where musicians are smiling and —

Oh my God yeah. The same with singing lyrics, oh yeah, absolutely. It’s part of the humanity, the humor. And if everything that you do in creative expression comes from your openness, then everything is in there. Always.
